title: Longest Common Subsequence
summary: Return the length of the longest subsequence common to both strings (0 if none).

perf.label: two 1,000-character strings
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(1000, "abcde"); String a1 = BCB.str(1000, "abcde");

statement:
Return the length of the longest common subsequence of `text1` and `text2`, or `0` if they share none.

A subsequence keeps the original order of characters but may skip some, so `"ace"` is a subsequence of `"abcde"`.
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: Compare the last characters. If they match, they can end the common subsequence; if not, one of them must be dropped.
L[i][j] = L[i − 1][j − 1] + 1 if text1[i − 1] == text2[j − 1], otherwise max(L[i − 1][j], L[i][j − 1]).
The table is (m + 1) × (n + 1) with zeros in row 0 and column 0. Two rows are enough for O(n) space.
explain: "ace" appears in both strings with its letters in order (a, c and e are picked from "abcde" skipping b and d). No longer common subsequence exists, so the answer is 3.

title: Delete Operation for Two Strings
summary: Each step deletes one character from either string. Return the fewest steps to make the two strings equal.

perf.label: two 500-character strings
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(500, "abc"); String a1 = BCB.str(500, "abc");

statement:
In one step you may delete exactly one character from either `word1` or `word2`. Return the minimum number of steps needed to make the two strings equal.

The strings end up equal to a common subsequence of both, so the fewest deletions keep their longest common subsequence: the answer is `len(word1) + len(word2) − 2 × LCS`.
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: The characters you keep form a common subsequence. To delete as little as possible, keep the longest one.
Compute the longest common subsequence L.
The answer is (word1.length − L) + (word2.length − L). A direct DP on deletions works too.
explain: Delete "s" from "sea" and "t" from "eat"; both become "ea". That takes 2 steps, the fewest possible.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
summary: Return a longest substring of s that is a palindrome. Any palindrome of the maximum length is accepted.
statement:
Return a longest contiguous substring of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards.

If several substrings share the maximum length, any of them is accepted.

A substring is contiguous: its characters sit next to each other in `s`. Every single character is a palindrome, so the answer is never empty.
constraints: `s` has only digits and English letters
hints: Every palindrome mirrors around its centre, and a centre is either one character or the gap between two.
For each of the 2n − 1 centres, expand outward while the characters on both sides match.
Keep the longest expansion. That is O(n²) time and O(1) space. A DP table isPal[i][j] also works, and Manacher's algorithm is O(n).
explain: "bab" reads the same both ways and no palindrome in "babad" is longer than 3. "aba" is just as long and would also be accepted; the example shows "bab".

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
summary: Return the length of the longest subsequence of s that is a palindrome.
statement:
Return the length of the longest subsequence of `s` that is a palindrome. A subsequence keeps the order of characters but may skip some.

For example in "cbbd" the longest palindromic subsequence is "bb", of length 2.
hints: Look at the two ends of the range s[i..j]. If they are equal, both can be in the palindrome.
P[i][j] = P[i + 1][j − 1] + 2 if s[i] == s[j], otherwise max(P[i + 1][j], P[i][j − 1]); P[i][i] = 1.
Fill by increasing length (or i from the end). It is also the LCS of s and reverse(s).
explain: Skipping the "a" leaves "bbbb", a palindrome of length 4. Keeping all five characters gives "bbbab", which is not a palindrome, so the answer is 4.

title: Palindromic Substrings
summary: Count the substrings of s that are palindromes (substrings at different positions count separately).
statement:
Count the substrings of `s` that are palindromes. Substrings at different positions are counted separately even if they contain the same characters.

For example "aaa" has 6 palindromic substrings: three single "a"s, two "aa"s and "aaa" itself.
hints: Every palindromic substring has a centre: a single character or the gap between two characters.
Expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres and count every step at which the two sides still match.
That counts each palindrome exactly once, in O(n²) time and O(1) space.
explain: The palindromic substrings of "abc" are "a", "b" and "c". No longer substring reads the same backwards, so the answer is 3.

title: Interleaving String
summary: Return whether s3 can be formed by interleaving s1 and s2, keeping each string's characters in their original order.

perf.label: 100 + 100 characters
perf.gen: String a0 = "a".repeat(100); String a1 = "a".repeat(99) + "b"; String a2 = "a".repeat(200);

statement:
Return `true` if `s3` can be formed by interleaving `s1` and `s2`: merging their characters into one string while keeping the characters of each in their original order.

For example, `"aadbbcbcac"` interleaves `"aabcc"` and `"dbbca"`.
constraints: All strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: If the lengths do not add up, the answer is false. Greedy matching fails when both strings could supply the next character.
ok[i][j] means "the first i characters of s1 and the first j of s2 can form the first i + j of s3".
explain: Split s1 as "aa" + "bc" + "c" and s2 as "dbbc" + "a". Alternating the pieces gives "aa" + "dbbc" + "bc" + "a" + "c" = "aadbbcbcac", which is s3, so the answer is `true`.

title: Edit Distance
summary: Return the fewest insertions, deletions and replacements of single characters that turn word1 into word2.

perf.label: two 500-character strings
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(500, "abcd"); String a1 = BCB.str(500, "abcd");

statement:
Return the minimum number of operations that turn `word1` into `word2`. Each operation inserts, deletes or replaces a single character.

For example turning "intention" into "execution" takes 5 operations. Each operation changes exactly one character.
constraints: Both strings have only lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the last characters of the prefixes word1[0..i) and word2[0..j). If they match, no operation is needed for them.
Otherwise D[i][j] = 1 + min(D[i − 1][j] (delete), D[i][j − 1] (insert), D[i − 1][j − 1] (replace)).
D[i][0] = i and D[0][j] = j. Two rows are enough.
explain: Replace "h" with "r" ("horse" → "rorse"), delete the second "r" ("rose"), then delete "e" ("ros"). Three operations, and no shorter sequence works, so the answer is 3.

title: Distinct Subsequences
summary: Return how many distinct subsequences of s equal t (the answer fits in 32 bits).
statement:
Return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` that equal `t`. Two subsequences are different if they use different positions of `s`.

The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

The characters of `t` must be matched in order, but they don't have to be next to each other in `s`.
constraints: Both strings have only English letters
hints: Count the ways to match t[0..j) using s[0..i). The new character s[i − 1] can be used for t[j − 1] if they are equal, or skipped.
With a one-dimensional array, update j from right to left. Intermediate values can exceed an int, so use a long or guard them.
explain: "rabbbit" has three b's and "rabbit" needs two of them. Skipping the first, second or third b gives 3 different choices of positions, so the answer is 3.

title: Regular Expression Matching
summary: Match the whole string s against pattern p, where "." matches any character and "*" matches zero or more of the preceding element.

perf.label: a pattern that defeats plain backtracking

statement:
Implement matching of a pattern `p` against the whole string `s` (not just a part of it), where:

- `.` matches any single character,
- `*` matches zero or more copies of the element just before it.

Every `*` in the pattern has a valid character or `.` before it.
constraints: `s` has only lowercase letters; `p` has lowercase letters, "." and "*"
hints: Plain recursion branches at every "*" and can take exponential time on patterns like "a*a*a*…c". Memoise it.
M[i][j] means s[i..] matches p[j..]. If p[j + 1] is "*", either skip "x*" (M[i][j + 2]) or, if s[i] matches x, consume one character (M[i + 1][j]).
Otherwise the characters must match and you move on: first-match && M[i + 1][j + 1]. The base case is the end of the pattern.
explain: The pattern "a" matches exactly one "a", but `s` is "aa" and the whole string must match. So the answer is `false`.
